introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800 (0760), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections (Section A: 1800 - 1922; Section B: 1922 - 1961; Section C: 1961 to present). All the questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 4 » par section (A : questions 1 à 4, B : 5 à 8, C : 9 à 12), c'est-à-dire le minimum imposé ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : « All the questions carry equal marks » et chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter). Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et texte en transparence du verso (illisible, sans rapport) ignorés ; aucune question coupée, aucune carte ni figure.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les dates et noms sont donnés de mémoire historique et sont à faire relire par un historien du Cameroun avant mise en ligne.

Les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `foumban conference of 1961`, `cameroon foreign policy under biya`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à recontrôler à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

Question 8 : le sujet ne donne pas les résultats ; le corrigé ne cite aucun nombre de sièges ni de voix (la répartition exacte des sièges entre KNDP et Alliance est à vérifier) et situe l'élection en janvier 1959 ; la nomination de Foncha (février 1959) est citée prudemment. L'explication par l'opinion sur le Nigeria et la réunification est l'interprétation courante, à nuancer.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Account for the defeat of the KNC-KPP Alliance in the 1959 elections in Southern Cameroons.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Southern Cameroons House of Assembly elections of January 1959 brought an end to the government of Dr E. M. L. Endeley, head of government since 1954 (Premier from 1958). Endeley's Kamerun National Congress (KNC) had joined the Kamerun People's Party (KPP) of N. N. Mbile in an alliance, but the Alliance was defeated by the Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP) of John Ngu Foncha, which won the majority of seats, and Foncha became Premier in February 1959. The defeat can be explained by the issue of the future of the territory, by the strengths of the KNDP and by the weaknesses of the Alliance.

**1. The central issue: the future of Southern Cameroons**
- By 1958 the question was what would happen to the territory when Nigeria became independent (scheduled for 1960). Endeley and the KNC had favoured a gradual path of autonomy and, in effect, a continuing association with Nigeria, in which Southern Cameroons would be a self-governing region within a Nigerian federation and have the right to review its position later.
- Foncha and the KNDP campaigned for *secession from Nigeria* and a separate path, with the aim of reunification with French Cameroon (later the Republic of Cameroon) or an independent Southern Cameroons. This policy appealed to the many voters who feared domination by Nigeria, and who identified with the idea of a Cameroonian nation.
- The campaign was therefore mainly fought on the issue of "Nigeria or Cameroon". Fear of Nigerian domination, of the Igbo and of the NCNC party of Eastern Nigeria favoured the KNDP, and the KNC-KPP Alliance was accused of being too close to Nigeria and of wishing to make Southern Cameroons a permanent part of it.

**2. Strengths of the KNDP**
- Foncha was a popular, modest and effective leader, a teacher from the Grassfields, with a strong following in Bamenda Province and good organisation at village level. The KNDP built on the northern Grassfields' sense of being neglected by the south and by Buea.
- The party offered a clear programme ("secession", reunification, an end to Nigerian control) and a positive vision for the Cameroons, backed by meetings, newspapers and the support of chiefs, farmers, women and the youth.
- The KNDP exploited the failures of the Endeley government, which were presented as examples of weakness, Nigerian influence and mismanagement of the economy, plantations and land questions.

**3. Weaknesses of the KNC-KPP Alliance**
- The Alliance was a marriage of convenience between two parties that had been bitter rivals, created in order to keep power, and it was widely seen as opportunistic. The KPP had split from the KNC in 1953, and the reunion was blamed on personal ambition.
- The Alliance suffered from internal disputes over candidates and tactics, and from loss of credibility with voters, as Endeley was seen as a leader too close to Nigeria and to the Eastern Region politicians.
- Its support was mainly concentrated in the coastal and forest areas (Victoria, Kumba), with the Bakweri and some other groups, and was too regional to win a majority. It was weak in the Grassfields.
- Its position on the future of the territory was less clear and less attractive than the KNDP's, and it lacked a strong answer to the demand for reunification.

**4. Other factors**
- Regional rivalry between the Grassfields of Bamenda and the coastal, forest regions of the south, which gave the KNDP a regional base that outweighed the Alliance's strongholds.
- The effect of events in the neighbouring territories: the independence of French Cameroon on 1 January 1960 was expected, and the independence of Nigeria promised.
- The first-past-the-post electoral system, which allowed a party with a modest lead in votes to win a majority of seats.

**Conclusion.** The KNC-KPP Alliance was defeated in 1959 mainly because most voters rejected its policy of staying close to Nigeria and preferred the KNDP's message of secession and reunification. The KNDP had a popular leader, a strong base in the Grassfields and an attractive programme, while the Alliance was divided, opportunistic and regionally weak. The result decided the future course of Southern Cameroons and led to the plebiscite of 1961.
